title: Designing Good Classes
summary: A good class has **one clear job**, a **small public interface that is hard to misuse**, **protects its invariants** and is **const-correct**. Design it from the point of view of the code that will use it.
markdown:
## From syntax to judgement You now know the mechanics of classes. This lesson is about using them well. None of it is enforced by the compiler; all of it decides whether your code is pleasant or painful to work with in six months. ```mermaid mindmap root((A good class)) One responsibility Its name says what it is Small interface Invariants Validated in the constructor Never exposed in a broken state Interface Actions, not getters and setters Hard to misuse explicit constructors Const correctness const member functions const reference parameters Value semantics Copies like an int Rule of Zero ``` ## One responsibility | Poor | Better | |---|---| | A `GameManager` that loads files, draws, reads input and keeps scores | `FileLoader`, `Renderer`, `InputHandler`, `ScoreBoard` | A class with one job is small enough to understand, test and reuse. A class with five jobs changes for five different reasons, and each change risks the other four. > [!tip] The one-sentence test > Describe the class in one sentence. If you need the word "and", it is probably two classes. ## Protect invariants for the object's whole life ```cpp class Percentage { public: explicit Percentage(int value) : m_value{ std::clamp(value, 0, 100) } {} void add(int delta) { m_value = std::clamp(m_value + delta, 0, 100); } int value() const { return m_value; } private: int m_value{}; // invariant: 0 <= m_value <= 100 }; ``` | Moment | How the invariant is kept | |---|---| | Creation | The constructor validates | | Every modification | Each member function that changes the data re-establishes the rule | | Outside the class | The data is private, so nothing else can touch it | Here invalid input is quietly brought into range. When invalid input should be reported as an error, the constructor throws an exception: [[9.05 Exceptions]]. ## Make the interface hard to misuse The best interface is one where the wrong call does not compile. | Easy to get wrong | Hard to get wrong | Technique | |---|---|---| | `Rectangle r{ 10, 20 };` | `Rectangle r{ Width{ 10 }, Height{ 20 } };` | A small type for each kind of value | | `Date d{ 11, 12, 2026 };` | `Date::fromYmd(2026, 11, 12)` | A named factory function | | `run(5.0)` accepted as a distance | `run(Meters{ 5.0 })` | An `explicit` constructor | ## Tell, do not ask ```cpp // Asking: pull the data out, decide outside, push it back. if (account.balance() >= amount) { account.setBalance(account.balance() - amount); } // Telling: ask the object to do it. The rule stays inside the class. if (!account.withdraw(amount)) { std::cout << "Insufficient funds\n"; } ``` In the first version, every caller must remember to check the balance. One who forgets breaks the invariant. In the second, forgetting is impossible. ## Const correctness | Check | | |---|---| | Every member function that does not modify the object is `const` | | | Parameters that are only read are `const T&`, or by value for cheap types | | | Members are returned by `const&` when callers only need to read them | | ## Struct or class? | Use a `struct` when | Use a `class` when | |---|---| | The members are independent of each other | The members must satisfy a rule together | | Every combination of values is valid | Some combinations are invalid | | `Point`, `Color`, `Config` | `Fraction`, `BankAccount`, `Date` | Do not wrap a plain bundle of data in getters and setters. It adds code without protecting anything. ## Value semantics and the Rule of Zero The easiest classes to use behave like `int`: they can be copied, assigned, compared and passed around freely, and each copy is independent. That behaviour is called **value semantics**. You get it for free when a class's members are themselves well-behaved: `std::string`, `std::vector`, other value types. The compiler-generated copy operations and destructor then do the right thing, and you write none of them. That is the **Rule of Zero**, and the next milestone explains why it matters: [[7.05 Move Semantics]]. ## A design process ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Write the code that
USES the class first"] --> B["List its actions
(the verbs)"] --> C["Decide the invariants"] --> D["Choose the private data"] --> E["Implement"] --> F["Test the edge cases"] ``` Starting from the calling code is the important step. It shows what the interface should feel like before any implementation detail has had the chance to shape it. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does "tell, do not ask" mean? - Always ask the user before changing data - Use public member variables instead of getters + Ask the object to act, rather than taking its data and deciding - Print a message every time a member function runs > `account.withdraw(50)` lets the account check its own rules. Reading the balance and setting it from outside spreads those rules everywhere. ? When is a plain struct better than a class? - When it has more than five members + When the data has no invariants to protect - When it needs a constructor - Never; classes are always better > If nothing can be invalid, there is nothing to protect, and public members are simpler. ? What is the one-sentence test? - A class should have one public function - A class should be written in one sentence of code + If describing a class needs "and", it may do too much - Every member function should be one line long > A class should do one job. Needing "and" to describe it is a sign to split it. ? What is the Rule of Zero? - A class should have zero public member variables - Never use `0` as a default value - Every class needs zero constructors + Use self-managing members, so no destructor or copies are written > Members such as `std::string` and `std::vector` clean up after themselves, so the compiler-generated operations are correct. ```
ideas:
Review one of your earlier classes against this lesson and fix what you find:
1. Member functions that should be `const`.
2. Setters that allow an invalid state.
3. Single-argument constructors that are not `explicit`.
4. Functions that do two jobs.

cards.q: What does "tell, do not ask" mean?
cards.a:
Ask the object to act, rather than taking its data and deciding

`account.withdraw(50)` lets the account check its own rules. Reading the balance and setting it from outside spreads those rules everywhere.

cards.q: When is a plain struct better than a class?
cards.a:
When the data has no invariants to protect

If nothing can be invalid, there is nothing to protect, and public members are simpler.

If describing a class needs "and", it may do too much

A class should do one job. Needing "and" to describe it is a sign to split it.

cards.q: What is the Rule of Zero?
cards.a:
Use self-managing members, so no destructor or copies are written

Members such as `std::string` and `std::vector` clean up after themselves, so the compiler-generated operations are correct.
